title: Nabataeans
capsule: The Nabataeans were an Arab trading people whose kingdom, centered on the rock-cut capital of Petra (Arabic: البتراء, al-Batrāʾ; Nabataean: Raqmu) in the Jordanian highlands, controlled the overland incense and spice routes linking Arabia, the Levant, and Egypt from at least the 4th century BCE. The kingdom reached its apex under Aretas IV (r. 9 BCE – 40 CE), the most prolific builder of Petra's monuments, and extended at times from the Sinai Peninsula to the Hejaz and into Hauran (southern Syria). Rome under Emperor Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom without recorded military resistance in 106 CE, converting it into the province of Arabia Petraea with Bosra as the new provincial capital; Petra subsequently declined as caravan routes shifted to Palmyra.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core territory around Petra and the major incense route corridors is well attested through archaeology and Greco-Roman sources; the outer limits of Nabataean political control in the Hejaz and Sinai are less precisely defined.
